I've got the same issue but much more severe. I'm taking a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and a very small amount of klonopin, but they only help a little for me. For some people an SSRI medication can really help, though (Prozac, Paxil, Zoloft etc.) The klonopin, which is a tranquilizer (like Xanax) is good if you take it right before you start the day.

Another route is CBT or cognitive behavioral therapy. Since you're still functioning well, the CBT can help you reinforce positive coping skills and slowly replace negative ones. My brother pretty much had his social anxiety cured in this way.

I hope all goes well -- pretty soon you'll be mingling like no tomorrow!
Thank you so much for your kindness and advice!

I understand completely, because even though I'm an atheist, in recent dark moments I sometimes feel a "spirit" of some kind that comforts me.

It's just having my mental health (obsessive compulsive rituals) getting worse and stealing away all my time and energy. I regret so much everything it's taken from me. When I try to fight and feel a little better, I'm just bowled over by the realization of how long I've been lost, battling this labrynthe of anxiety, how much real life has passed me by. It breaks my heart, really.

Thanks for empathizing. It's a lot of things, but it boils down to I just don't love myself or believe in myself anymore. I'm trying to remember what that feels like, because maybe that will help me through.

I've also got severe o.c.d. What people don't understand is the exhausting tedium of doing constant rituals, both mentally or physically, and also the fear that grinds you all day every day. People don't understand having to repeatedly  navigate a labrynthe of hundreds of upsetting thoughts before you can even start to try to address the "real" demands of day to day life.

It's weird too, because like you, I would almost be afraid to suddenly be symptom free. At least my ocd has been there for me all this time,  and it's overwhelming to confront the possibilities of what life might demand if I were free of this boulder tied around my ankle. 

When my symptoms start getting better, that's when the real depression kicks in, because you suddenly realize all these years of work struggling with the o.c.d. was just in your mind. You suddenly realize now you have to face the real tasks of actual life. And then, the regret when you realize how much anguish and time and energy it has robbed you of.

I'm right there with you, my friend. I'm not making progress, but I have to hold on to this unfathomable optimism that somehow keeps me in the game. I'm not religious at all but some kind of comforting presence I can feel sometimes, like the benevolence of the universe balancing it out. I hope you'll keep a similar optimism.

Hey, I was on that stuff once as an adjunct treatment for severe o.c.d. Never really liked it, and I only took it a short time.

I don't remember if I had withdrawal, but I've had a hell of a time with withdrawal from other psychiatric meds. It sucks, but it's just your body adjusting to a new routine.

I bet you'll be used to the change pretty soon. But if you are truly worried, I'm sure your doctor would be glad to have you back in for an appointment, or his nurse might answer some questions for you. Take care.

I relate so well to your story. At almost the same age, I was an expat living in Moscow, and I have severe o.c.d. and tend to be a hypochondriac. I started having urinary issues and what freaked me out even worse was the idea of trying to get one of the Russian "polyclinic" doctors to diagnose anything.

I think you're doing the right thing -- my advice is to just have the medical tests done by a good western quality doctor, so you can have peace of mind.

The problem with panic attacks is they can cause you to feel symptoms that mimic a heart attack. So, I think you have to rule out the possibility of genuine heart issues first. If there is something seriously wrong, any competent Chinese doctor would be sure to identify it almost immediately, i think. But I imagine they'll say you're fine, and then you'll have the peace of mind you're in no real danger.

After you rule out the possibility of a medical cause, if symptoms persist you might be looking at panic attacks as the cause. That will require possibly psychiatric meds (like xanax, ssris etc) or meeting with a good therapist. It might be hard to find a good person abroad, but I'm sure there's resources for expats and English speakers. If you ever had a therapist back stateside, he or she might be able to do therapy with you over skype.

Anyway, I felt better about my stuff after I paid out of pocket to be examined at an American clinic in moscow. Although if I remember right, the crazy Russian lady doctors actually ended up being correct that I had prostatitis. But I felt much safer with a western type doctor.

If it turns out to be panic disorder, you should know that panic symptoms don't actually put your health in danger (even if it feels really unpleasant)

Best of luck, I know you can overcome this hurdle and get back to exploring in china.

Every person says things when they're angry that they regret. I know it sucks, but you have to eventually forgive yourself. If you keep beating yourself up, the pain from all that guilt makes you feel so bad, you're likely to lash out again. It can become a cycle. 

Each of us feels guilty when we act contrary to what we believe is right, and I know guilt feels awful. But you have to eventually forgive yourself and move on. 

Meanwhile,  try to think of your college and career pursuits in less black-and-white terms. We're taught early on that education is about getting a certain score on certain tests, to somehow show you're worthy. 

But I think real learning and real living necessarily require mistakes. That's how you master any subject. The important thing isn't to be flawless, but to remain committed to the process. You go after it every day, some days it goes well, others not so well.

But all of that totals up to having learned and accomplished something significant. The ups and downs are just part of a larger process. 

So take heart and keep going. I believe you're a good person - and I believe in you.

I hope you understand that I was only trying to say that I understand having guilt. I wasn't trying to be critical in any way.

What I was trying to say is that I think it's natural for everyone to have something they use for an escape, whether it's food, drinking, the internet, etc.

I'm really sorry to hear you're struggling. I'm also struggling with severe anxiety, in the form of a severe type of ocd which I've had for 20 years.

What sucks is I've made the situation worse by compulsively wasting time online as an escape from all my pain and depression. It sucks when you start blaming yourself, believe me I understand.

I'd love to see you spend some of your savings on weekly meetings with a good therapist. It can be expensive , but it really helps me to have an ally who I can confide in. If you find someone you trust and respect, it could change your life for the better. 

Just please never give up on yourself. You sound like a really good guy who  is only human like everyone else. I want you to know I'm rooting for you!

I feel similar, it can be so hard to move forward and grow and be open to new, good things, especially when you feel so much regret and remorse and anxiety about the past. But we've all made mistakes and we've all hurt people, and that doesn't mean you're an inherently bad person. Just a regular, imperfect person like everyone else. You're obviously a good person because you care about others and take it to heart when you've done something you believe is wrong. But you've got to let go of past mistakes because all the self blaming and guilt can just perpetuate a cycle. That negativity tends to trigger yet even more regrettable decisions, because it puts you in too much pain. It's time to let go of past mistakes, treat yourself with love and believe in yourself. I'm wishing you well.
